Organisations with OSPO-like support functions Organisations with OSPO-like support functions have no formal tie to PSOs through ownership or membership. They support OSS’s adoption, development, and collaboration through their own means. This study has investigated the case of Code for Romania, a not-forprofit civil society organisation without formal ties to PSOs and which is primarily funded through grants, donations, and sponsorships. #### 4.6.1. Providing support for design and execution of OSS strategies Being an independent and non-government OSPO, Code for Romania does not provide support on the design and execution of OSS strategies for any PSO. Their aim is rather to equip civil society and PSOs with OSS tools and solutions to enable them to provide better public services. Developed solutions should work and be at par with the requirements of institutional users. They see a general need for a core of systems needed by a more extensive set of PSOs, for example, regarding websites, registration systems, building registries, and complaint management. #### 4.6.2. Providing support for use and adoption of OSS Code for Romania generally encourages and promotes the use of internally developed OSS projects in collaboration with stakeholders and end-users. They today provide a set of about 50 different applications. These applications relate to areas such as education, citizen engagement, health care, the environment, and social services. All applications are maintained and offered as hosted services primarily for PSOs within Romania. If other countries are interested, they must run their own instances. #### 4.6.3. Providing support for development and release of OSS Code for Romania mainly considers external OSS projects as building blocks to their internally developed OSS projects. A primary reason is that they feel the externally developed solutions are generally not ready for production by a PSO, for example, in terms of quality, performance, and accessibility. Code for Romania works on putting the pieces together, raising the bar, and tailoring to public sector requirements. One exception mentioned regards Consul, a citizen-engagement platform originating from the City of Madrid is one example. Generally, any modifications or development of upstream projects are contributed back. #### 4.6.4. Developing and managing key OSS applications Code for Romania focuses on developing OSS tools and applications for needs addressing critical use cases in society, working closely with concerned stakeholder. The team has also developed a suite of about 30 OSS solutions targeting the humanitarian refugee situation that emerged due to the conflict in Ukraine. The solutions provide a common interface for the refugees entering Romania, for example, to apply for emergency housing, health services, women, and mother and child services specifically. Some solutions are managed by PSOs, for example, related to housing allocation. Others are managed by different civil society organisations designated with different responsibilities. Some of the solutions have been replicated internationally, including Moldova. In total, about 1.5 million refugees have been using the different services up until today. Another notable example of an OSS-based solution regards a website builder for public institutions, which was initiated through research and collaboration with small and large municipalities to identify core needs. One key issue was that all municipalities needed a website. Often, the municipalities procured a solution and ended up in a lockin situation, having to pay for smaller website updates. The website builder is now available in two versions, one for municipalities and one for national administrations, as they have different needs and regulations to abide by. The goal is to hand the solution over to the Agency for Digital Government, who in turn will support PSOs on different levels to adopt the tool. Code for Romania will, however, continue to develop and maintain the tool. #### 4.6.5. Providing supporting for licence selection and monitoring All software developed is released primarily under the MPL2.0 licence. #### 4.6.6. Analysing and following up on OSS adoption and evolution Code for Romania works actively with metrics and has it as a core design principle on their checklist (inc. documentation and other OSS hygiene aspects). It enables them to validate their hypotheses and verify that the products work as intended. They also require that PSOs provide the necessary data when one of their solutions is being used. The data is kept on an aggregated and anonymised level. In one case, the collected data and overarching metrics helped identify certain instances of a housing allocation app among municipalities that were not working correctly. #### 4.6.7. Communicating and managing relations with the external OSS ecosys- tem Code for Romania has extensive collaboration with other ‘‘Code4’’ organisations across the globe. Code for Romania is, however, considered the most advanced in terms of building solutions. All the Code4 organisations come together under an international organisation called Commit Global, where they share knowledge and collaborate across borders. #### 4.6.8. Provisioning of training and education on OSS Code for Romania has a program focused on supporting OSS policies, connecting PSOs with experts, and training potential employees in government and existing staffers in parallel as they explore and develop new needs and OSS-based solutions for those. The OSPO representative notes that the organisation is generally observing an increase in interest among policymakers and PSOs. Working together with stakeholders and users early on and showcasing solutions is considered to promote adoption and interest. Code for Romania is, however, not to be considered an advocacy group. Discussion As in industry (Haddad, 2020), we noted several ways in which OSPOs can be organised. The findings specifically revealed six distinct archetypes of OSPOs, each with its organisational characteristics and means of supporting OSS operations within the public sector. The archetypes vary and overlap both in structure and responsibilities (see Tables 3 and 4, respectively). Considering OSS strategy and policy, National government OSPOs act as mediators between policy and practice, translating national strategies into actionable support and guidance. Local and Institution-centric OSPOs adapt these strategies to fit local or organisational priorities, not always explicitly, but more abstractly in the context of digital transformation and innovation. The associations, in turn, enable collectives of PSOs to codify and share strategy, while Academic and OSPOlike entities are shaped by external review, research, and commercial objectives. Here, procurement-related support is of specific importance (Cassell, 2008; Deller and Guilloux, 2008) as the lack of knowledge and practice in navigating complex legal frameworks in relation to software and OSS acquisition is a recognised challenge (Lundell et al., 2021), and can lead to lock-in (Lundell et al., 2022) if not done properly (Persson and Linåker, 2024). In the Institution-centric cases, which have more similar operations to industry contexts, the focus is more on enabling engineers to be autonomous in the intake of OSS components, while managing both legal and security-related risks that arise. Development and release of OSS also draws a line between useroriented and engineering-oriented organisations, as well as the support required by each. Institution-centric OSPOs generally have well-defined processes, tools, and infrastructure to support their engineers, while National, Local, and Association-based OSPOs are more geared towards providing guidelines, high-level procurement-centric support, and common infrastructure such as national social coding platforms, a critical enabler for open collaboration (Mergel, 2015). The latter group of OSPOs and their overarching organisations can still prove engineering-heavy, stewarding and maintaining key applications for the public sector at large. Association-based OSPOs (similar to OSS foundations (O’Mahony, 2005)) are especially well-suited as long-term bodies, as also exemplified in the literature (Frey, 2023; Viseur and Jullien, 2023; Persson and Linåker, 2024). Still, examples across the national and local also show how single PSOs can take on a stewardship role (Linåker et al., 2025). Regardless of context, the Open rather than the Inner Source way was a preferred means for collaboration. Across both adoption and development, license compliance and legal support plays a critical role, with various types of OSPOs providing similar support for tool automation and practical advice as needed. The former is more prominent in cases where engineering departments are present. The latter is more exclusively in scope, e.g., in Academic OSPOs, as they provide guidance related to commercial or project-related requirements and grant application writing. Metrics and follow-up are generally considered necessary, but practices are applied to a much lesser degree across the archetypes. Use cases include advocacy, signalling impact, and the need for continued funding. More resourceful organisations and OSPOs are more open to formal and tool-supported approaches, while those more resourceconstrained rely on ad hoc reporting, tacit knowledge, or opportunistic internal surveys, with follow-up being less formalised. Community management and outreach is practised by most types of OSPOs, whether through national/international networks, industry, or other municipalities, recognising the importance of leveraging communities and open collaboration to benefit from many of the opportunities OSS can offer. Communities of practice, advisory councils, intra-PSO partnerships, and national and international OSPO networks are some examples. The OSPOs become both an interface and boundary spanner (Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015), enabling knowledge transfer and dissemination across an internal and external workforce. The Journal of Systems & Software 241 (2026) 112998 18 Training and education is also more or less practised across the various OSPOs as cases highlight a consistent and recognised need for maturing knowledge and capabilities, aligning with literature (Marco- Simó and Pastor-Collado, 2020; Borg et al., 2018). The actual delivery, however, ranges from comprehensive, structured programs for well-resourced OSPOs to informal peer support or reliance on external communities in less resourceful cases. Topics of concern range from business models and open science principles (in case of Academic OSPOs), to procurement and governance (e.g., in case of Local government OSPOs). In general, deviances in support provided relate to the resource intensity, and observed need for OSS as a strategic means in relation to the OSPOs’ overarching organisations’ general policy and business goals. National government, Institution-centric, and Association-based OSPOs exhibit the highest degree of structural professionalisation, with formal frameworks, standardised approaches, and sustainability planning, while local and Academic OSPOs show greater adaptiveness, granularity, and bespoke support, but also more direct capacity constraints. Organisations with OSPO-like support functions, such as Coding for Romania, coming from the civil society, demonstrate sectoral innovation and community translation but are usually not embedded in any formal PSO-driven governance and collaboration structures. The type of support provided accordingly relates to the reliance of external resources, which is much more significant for the PSOs within the local levels of government, in contrast to the more resourceful PSOs with the National government or Institution-centric OSPOs (aligning with others’ observations (Linåker et al., 2025)). Comparing the industry (Haddad, 2020), the latter archetype is the one most in line with established templates, given its mainly internal focus and support from a typically large IT workforce in its OSS adoption. The National government OSPOs surveyed showed a higher emphasis on supporting other PSOs across various parts and levels of government. Compared to the more organisation-centric focus of industry OSPOs (Haddad, 2020), our investigation further shows, across the archetypes, that there is a will and need to support each other within the public sector in the collective adoption of OSS, even though certain OSPOs may have more of an inward focus. This especially resonated on the local level of government, where, for example, municipalities have significant differences in capabilities and resources (Frey, 2023; Viseur and Jullien, 2023). Those more capable fill an essential role in leading OSS initiatives and adoption (Linåker et al., 2025). They should be encouraged and supported to establish Local government OSPOs that, in turn, can act as accelerators and supporters for other local governments (including municipalities, cities, and regions). In particular, Association-based OSPOs enable less capable PSOs, especially at the local government level, to collaborate and initiate OSS solutions by addressing everyday needs. The associations act as OSS Stewards (Persson and Linåker, 2024), providing a sustainable hosting and maintenance of OSS projects on neutral grounds similar to general OSS foundations and their often industry-driven OSS projects (O’Mahony, 2005). The associations further create a collective, more informed voice towards vendors, who are critical for both the adoption of OSS solutions (Lungo and Kaasbøl, 2007; Koloniaris et al., 2018) and their sustainability (Shaikh, 2016). The associations (as other OSPOs) accordingly also provide quality assurance in verifying necessary OSS practices are used (Mergel, 2016), so lock-in can be avoided (Persson and Linåker, 2024). A common feature across the cases was also the leveraging of external communities and knowledge networks to exchange best practices, grow collaborations, and use as a force multiplier in the development of OSS projects - again highlighting the role of OSPOs as boundary spanners (Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015). Civil society, volunteers and enthusiasts across sectors commonly played a key role in these communities. Civil society specifically fills a gap by enabling the use of OSS and helping to organise PSOs, both in the collaborative development of projects and towards a joint National government OSPO. PSOs should, hence, not only look to themselves but also to the rest of society for support and input. The OSPOs across the different archetypes can complement each other, forming a larger community where they collaborate and exchange resources and knowledge, building and scaling institutional capacity on a societal level. ### 5.1. Implications for practice The study provides practitioners with knowledge and examples to use as a basis when considering and designing support structures to enable the implementation of OSS-related policies and strategies. Based on our findings, we provide the following recommendations for national governments: • National digital transformation agendas should formally incorpo- rate OSS as a fundamental tool for realising policy objectives. • The creation of National government OSPOs is essential to coordi- nate the implementation of OSS within national digital strategies and maximise their impact. • PSOs should be assisted in aligning their own digital transfor- mation strategies with national OSS ambitions, including the establishment of dedicated OSPOs to deliver on these goals. • Cross-sectoral collaboration should be enhanced through the for- mation and facilitation of national-level public sector OSS and OSPO networks, aimed at fostering knowledge exchange and joint action. • Comprehensive guidance should be developed, specifying circum- stances and best practices for the consideration, acquisition, and creation of OSS by PSOs. • Investments are needed to develop specialised education and training programmes to expand OSS expertise within the public sector workforce and among technology suppliers. • Active participation from civil society organisations should be supported and encouraged, recognising their essential role in advancing public sector OSS adoption and collaboration. • National OSS-related performance indicators should be integrated into broader digital governance frameworks to monitor progress and reinforce accountability in digital transformation efforts. For Local governments (including Municipalities, Cities, and Regions), we make the following recommendations: • Local governments should articulate and adopt OSS strategies tailored to their specific objectives, local contexts, and available resources. • The establishment of local OSPOs is recommended to ensure that OSS strategies are realised and embedded within municipal or regional digital agendas. • Mechanisms should be established, such as associations or joint legal-administrative entities, for pooling expertise and resources across localities to jointly govern, procure, and sustain OSS-based projects. • Larger or more resource-rich municipalities should adopt a lead- ership role in guiding and supporting smaller counterparts in leveraging OSS for digital change. • Civil society involvement should be enabled and encouraged to enhance public sector capability and promote broader community engagement in OSS adoption and development. Finally, for Higher Education and Research Institutions, we make the following recommendations: • Universities and research organisations should provide clear pol- icy guidance on the strategic role of OSS in advancing their institutional missions. The Journal of Systems & Software 241 (2026) 112998 19 • Researchers must be supported through infrastructure, advice, and training in using OSS for research collaboration, dissemination, and broader impact. • Technology Transfer Offices are encouraged to promote OSS as a pathway for commercialising research and building sustainable business models around academic outputs. • The role and value of OSS outputs should be recognised in re- search assessment, including in hiring, promotion, programme design, and funding allocation processes. • Collaboration between Academic OSPOs and PSOs should be actively fostered, both nationally and across Europe. • European research institutions should study and learn from in- ternational best practices in developing and scaling Academic OSPOs, to ensure global competitiveness and local impact. ### 5.2. Implications for research The study has several limitations, including opportunities for future research. Among these is the generalisability and transferability of the presented results, which the reader must consider alongside the contextual factors at play in the various cases studied and how they together form a representation of the OSPO archetypes. The roles and responsibilities within the OSPOs will depend on the specific organisation and their own direction and goals for leveraging OSS, as defined by their OSS strategy or policy. By studying additional cases, future research can help clarify the nuances of the respective archetypes and how they may change, as well as their naming and the addition of other archetypes. Our broad sampling provides a foundation of knowledge for research to depart from in further investigating the role of OSS and open technologies at large as tools and vehicles for digital transformation and innovation in the public sector and governments. Specifically, we encourage future research to explore: • the impact of different OSPO archetypes and practices on public sector digital transformation outcomes. Such research can shed light on which structures and processes deliver the greatest value in different contexts. • how OSPOs translate national or organisational OSS policies and strategies into concrete action, and what kinds of policy instruments, goals, and incentive structures foster actual systemic uptake of OSS across the various parts of government and public sector. • what factors enable some OSPOs to scale and professionalise their support, and what type of support proves most efficient across the OSPO archetypes and the context they support. • other types of OSPO archetypes, for example, considering trans- national contexts with countries, lacking incentives and resources to develop their own support structures. • how OSPO archetypes and practices differ (or not) in low- and middle-income countries, and what barriers and challenges, as well as opportunities and potential that OSS offers, compared to more developed contexts. • how maturity and extent of support structures for OSS in govern- ment can be measured and followed up through digital government indices to help steer countries on a path towards achieving their policy goals. • how OSPO archetypes and practices must adapt and consider other forms of open technologies, including open and shared data, open science, open hardware, and open source AI. ## 6. Conclusions To sum up, we note that OSPOs come in many shapes and colours, and not always with the OSPO label. In general terms, they represent a support function, a policy enabler, and a change agent that drive of culture and organisational change, helping to address the fundamental fears and challenges implied by the openness, for example, in terms of viral licenses, usability, customisation needs, security concerns and lack support. The OSPO helps organisations acknowledge and manage these fears and challenges in a grounded and pragmatic way. The OSPO helps organisations to weigh the risks and costs against the benefits and potential of going open. The OSPO provide organisations with the necessary tools and introducing the best practices to leverage OSS as a tool to achieve their business or policy goals. The latter is an important characteristic to highlight as establishing an OSPO without an overarching strategy or plan is of limited use. Equally, it is as meaningless to define an OSS strategy or policy without ensuring that there is sufficient knowledge, support, understanding, and infrastructure to implement the strategy or policy. In essence, the OSPO can be considered a policy enabler and support action, enabling an PSOs to reach the different policy goals, be it sovereignty, interoperability or innovation. As a change agent, the OSPO would ideally dissipate with time as an organisation transforms and grows the capabilities required to leverage OSS accordingly, a phenomenon that has lately been observed in the IT industry. However, looking forward, we do not anticipate this trend anytime soon in the public sector. Rather, there is a need to widen the scope and focus beyond OSS, which can easily become siloed as that of open data. To achieve policy goals and the strive towards a more digitally sovereign, interoperable, and open society, scope and focus of policies and strategies, as of the OSPOs, need to include the data, the standards for how it is represented and communicated, the APIs between systems and their environments, the hardware it all runs on, and the science that drives the development forward. OSPOs will, hence, continue to play a pivotal role going forward, although the meaning of ’’Open Source’’ will most likely move beyond software towards open technologies in society at large. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement Johan Linåker: Writing – review & editing, Writing – original draft, Visualization, Validation, Supervision, Software, Resources, Project administration, Methodology, Investigation, Funding acquisition, Formal analysis, Data curation, Conceptualization. France In France, the national OSPO is constituted by the Free Software Unit, comprising a team of three individuals, located at the French Interministerial Digital Directorate (Direction interministérielle du Numérique - La DINUM). The OSPO’s primary focus is on supporting PSOs under the various ministries within the national level of government. They also have an implicit mandate to support the Directorate internally in terms of OSS. The OSPO was established in 2021 following a number of laws, decrees, and strategies that promote digital sovereignty, transparency, and trust in the public sector. France’s first Open Government Partnership National Action Plan (2015) commits the French government to promoting open government principles, including transparency, participation, and collaboration. In 2016, The French Law for a Digital Republic required PSOs to preserve the control, durability, and independence of their information systems. It also encouraged the use of free software and open formats in the development, purchase, or use of these systems (Article 9 of The Law ’’pour une République numérique’’, sometimes called ’’Loi Lemaire’’). More directly linked to the formation of the OSPO, the so-called Bothorel Report (Mission Bothorel, 2021) recommended that the French government establish a national OSPO. The report argued that OSS is a key enabler of digital sovereignty and innovation, and that the government should do more to promote its use in the public sector. A.1.2. Italy In Italy, the OSPO is represented by the Developers Italia project, founded in 2017 and jointly managed by the Department for Digital Transformation (Dipartimento per la Trasformazione Digitale) and the Agency for Digital Italy (Agenzia per l’Italia digitale). The initiative stems from the requirements of the country’s law on digital public administration dating back to 2012. Article 68 of the ’Code for the Digital Administration’ instructs public administrations to consider software ’’in the category of free and open-source software’’. The law now mandates public administrations to consider using OSS when procuring software solutions. The OSPO’s support extends across all levels of government. Within the Department, Developers Italia is managed by a smaller team within the Department’s engineering group, focusing on providing technical support and services related to enabling OSS use and development. On the Agency for Digital Italy’s side, the focus is on providing legal advice and related support. A.1.3. Germany In Germany, the OSPO is constituted by the Centre for Digital Sovereignty (Zentrum Digitale Souveränität), a PSO currently under the Federal Ministry of the Interior since the end of 2022. The ambition, however, is to include different German states as owners in the future. Currently, the Centre for Digital Sovereignty is in a build-up phase, being piloted by a smaller team of individuals, with the goal of expanding to a size of 67 people in the near future. The formation of the German OSPO can be traced back to a 2019 study by the German federal government highlighting the risks of depending on a few IT suppliers, emphasising increased costs and reduced autonomy. This concern was echoed in a joint paper by the federal Chief Information Officer (CIO), IT-Planning Council, and IT- Council, all aiming to enhance digital sovereignty. By 2022, the new coalition government’s 178-page agreement, ’’Daring More Progress’’, was released after extensive negotiations (Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands (SPD), Die Grünen und Freie Demokraten (FDP), 2025). It emphasised the role of OSS in enhancing digital infrastructure and government services, considering it vital for digital sovereignty. Furthermore, Germany’s third national action plan (2021–2023) under the Open Government Partnership focused on OSS, mentioning initiatives like the Corona-Warn-App. The plan also detailed actions intended to promote the objectives of the cross-government initiative, including the establishment of the National government OSPO, the Centre for Digital Sovereignty. Mission Bothorel, 2021），但並沒有正式的建議或要求。儘管如此，已有多個 OSPO 案例被報導，涵蓋超國家層級（例如 European Commission1）、國家層級（例如 Italy2）、區域層級（例如 Galicia3）與地方層級（例如 Paris4）的政府，也包括國營企業（例如 Alliander5）、學術界（例如 Trinity College Dublin6）以及國際人道組織（例如 WHO7）。其中，後者特別是在 OSPO 如何協助因應人道與社會挑戰的脈絡下受到重視，並透過聯合國每年舉辦的 OSPOs for Good conference 呈現。8 這些案例並不一致使用 OSPO 這個標籤，但它們都具備相似特徵，可與 OSPO 概念的多種定義相互對照（The TODO Group, 2024a）。 關於 OSPO 如何架構與組織，以及它們承擔哪些責任，目前研究仍僅限於少數值得注意的案例。Herpig（2023）探討網路安全 OSPO 可以如何設置為整體公部門 OSPO 的一部分，或是在國家資安機關內部的獨立單位。這類 OSPO 的重點包括「供應鏈安全政策工作，[以及] 協調政府機關與辦公室，確保開源軟體（OSS）安全不再受限於危機循環」。OpenForum Europe（OpenForum Europe, 2022b）主要從政策角度探討四個公部門 OSPO 案例，凸顯其所屬公部門組織（PSO）的基礎目標與策略。Linux Foundation（Linux Foundation, 2024）調查歐洲公部門的 OSS 現況，並根據多位 OSPO 受訪者的觀察，強調 OSPO 是推動 OSS 營運與採用的關鍵促成因素。然而，這些報告都沒有就公部門整體應如何設計 OSPO 提供指引，也沒有納入政府層級、資源與政策目標等情境因素。現有指南與資源偏向實務導向，針對一般 OSPO 或組織在將 OSS 視為策略性倡議時，可能承擔的治理、流程與任務提供指引（The 1 https://interoperable-europe.ec.europa.eu/collection/ec-ospo 2 https://developers.italia.it/ 3 https://mancomun.gal/es/ 4 https://open source.paris.fr/ossparis/english.html 5 https://www.alliander.com/en/open-source/ 6 https://www.tcd.ie/innovation/for-trinity-innovators/open-sourceprogramme-office/ 7 https://pandemichub.who.int/ 8 https://www.un.org/digital-emerging-technologies/content/ospos-good- 2024 TODO Group, 2024a; Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015）。 研究也進一步聚焦於探索 OSS 解決方案的採用，例如組織從專有軟體轉向 OSS 替代方案的轉型（Silic and Back, 2017；Waring and Maddocks, 2005），以及辨識並評估可能的效益、風險與挑戰（Koloniaris et al., 2018；Deller and Guilloux, 2008）。既有研究凸顯的一般因素包括：對技術支援的明確需求（Oram, 2011）、採購相關支援（Shaikh, 2016；Mergel, 2016），以及政策制定者持續且具策略性的承諾（Cassell, 2008；Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015）。後者很容易因公共辯論與政府更迭而消散（Maldonado, 2010）。本研究透過 OSPO 架構，探討如何特別藉由組織支援職能或能力中心，促成 OSS 的採用、開發與協作，以回應研究與實務上的缺口。本研究奠基於作者的一份基礎報告；該報告由歐盟執委會數位服務總司（Directorate-General for Digital Services, DIGIT）委託 OpenForum Europe 與 RISE，在 OSOR 專案下透過與 Wavestone SA 簽訂的 Specific Contract 32 FWC DI/07929 執行。因此，本研究明確聚焦於歐盟（EU）、挪威、列支敦斯登與冰島境內的公共部門組織（PSO），如何支持並促成 OSS 的使用、開發與協作。本研究採取質性研究方法，訪談調查了 16 個不同公共部門 OSPO 案例中的 18 位 OSPO 代表。這些案例經過交叉分析，並被分類為六種 OSPO 原型，概述各原型中的 OSPO 如何組織、其職責內容，以及它們如何在各自的範圍與領域內支持 OSS。研究發現並透過兩場後續焦點團體加以驗證與補充；參與者包括先前的受訪者與其他專家。我們提出以下貢獻： • 一套以實證為基礎的 OSPO 原型與實務類型學，可引導 PSO 在考量自身脈絡、資源與政策目標時，設計自己的 OSPO。 • 針對政策提出建議，以實作支援結構與計畫，發揮 OSS 作為數位創新與主權工具所帶來的潛力。 • 為未來數位治理奠定基礎並提出若干方向。 研究，探討在公部門各種情境中，如何支持 OSS 政策的落實。由於本研究屬於質性研究，讀者在進行任何軼事式概括之前，應特別考量各個報告案例的脈絡描述。此外，本文提出的 OSPO 原型，是根據有限的研究案例樣本所建構，只能呈現公部門 OSPO 可能如何組織與架構的部分圖像。每個 OSPO 都會因其所屬組織的文化、關注重點與實務做法而有所不同。即便如此，本文提出的原型仍可為實務工作者與研究者提供靈感來源與設計知識。本報告其餘部分的架構如下：首先介紹背景與相關研究，接著在此基礎上提出概念框架，作為本研究的先驗架構（見第 2 節）。接著介紹研究設計，並討論本研究效度可能面臨的威脅（見第 3 節）。之後的結果章節會呈現 OSPO 原型，以及對所研究案例的交叉分析（見第 4 節），最後則依據研究發現提出討論與結論（見第 5 節）。The Journal of Systems & Software 241 (2026) 112998 2 ## 2. 背景與相關研究 以下將介紹本研究的背景與相關研究，這些內容構成本研究的脈絡並提供參考，同時也說明作為後續研究基礎與框架的概念框架。首先，本文會根據一組既有資料來源，界定什麼構成一個 OSPO。接著概述在產業脈絡中，OSPO 可能如何架構、可能包含哪些角色，以及 OSPO 可能承擔哪些責任。其後，本文會引用一份較早從公共政策觀點探討公部門 OSPO 的報告，提供相關脈絡。最後，本文會簡要介紹概念框架。 ### 2.1. OSPO 的定義是什麼？ 開源專案辦公室（Open Source Program Office, OSPO）作為一種組織形式，其概念源自 2000 年代初期的產業界，當時主要出現在 Sun Microsystems、Hewlett-Packard、Intel 與 Google 等較大型、軟體密集的公司之中（Ruff, 2022; Phipps, 2021）。自那時起，隨著軟體產業以外的若干組織與產業也開始採用這種組織形式，這個概念也逐漸發展並成熟（The TODO Group, 2024c）。隨著 OSPO 的成長，對於 OSPO 是什麼的定義與看法也隨之增加。產業網絡 The TODO Group 將 OSPO 描述為「一個組織開源營運與架構的能力中心」，其職責可能包括設計並協助推動開源軟體（OSS）選用與導入流程、合規與稽核、貢獻與社群參與，以及為組織內不同利害關係人提供訓練（The TODO Group, 2024a）。OSPO Alliance（例如由 OW2、Eclipse Foundation、OpenForum Europe 與 Foundation for Public Code 共同發起的倡議）則認為 OSPO 是「一個跨職能團隊，用來協助定義並引導組織的開源管理策略與組織準備度」（OSPO Alliance, 2021）。兩個網絡都同意，OSPO 並沒有「一體適用」的模式。相反地，其任務與職責會依據上層組織的目標、策略，以及對 OSS 的看法而有所不同。從公部門角度來看，這個概念仍在形成之中，而且常以不同名稱出現，儘管其意涵相近。舉例來說，OpenForum Europe 將其視為「一種制度性的組織建制，支持並加速開源軟體的使用、創造與應用」（OpenForum Europe, 2022b）。具體而言，他們強調的是「以策略性方式工作，以達成該機構與開源交會的政策目標」，這與產業 OSPO 的商業觀點形成對比。不過，從一般角度來看，其重點仍然與促成 OSS 成為創造價值的工具有關，而這種價值創造是基於核心組織的目標，無論該組織屬於公部門或私部門。因此，OSPO++ 這個由大學、政府與公民機構中的協作型 OSPO 所組成的網絡與社群，也從公部門角度看待這種組織建制，並強調市政、政府與大學等場域。 他們思考公共部門脈絡相較於私人部門脈絡，可能帶來不同的組織結構、誘因，以及官僚層級（Dillon and Litthauer, 2020）。常見的外包與取得技術能力趨勢（Mikalsen and Farshchian, 2020），再加上同樣具有徵兆性的短期規劃與避險文化（Alanne et al., 2015），進一步增添了可能影響 PSO 中 OSPO 如何成形的細微差異。考量到這些細微差異，本研究使用 OSPO construct 來研究 PSO 如何支持並促成其自身在 OSS 使用、開發與協作相關能力上的成長。因此，本研究的分析單位是 PSO 所提供的支持功能，不受其組織方式或被稱為何種標籤所限制。 ### 2.2. 產業中的 OSPO 結構 OSPO 的結構與組織位置會依其目標與目的而有所不同。Haddad（2020）提出五種 OSPO 在產業環境中可能的設置方式（見表 1）。如下表所示，這些例子在內部支持者、預算、人員配置、支援對象，以及適用的組織規模上各有差異。第一個例子是將 OSPO 設在研發組織內，並由高階管理層直接支持與督導。這樣的設置讓 OSPO 與產品部門隔離，使其能執行整體的開源軟體（OSS）策略，而不受特定產品策略所限制。同時，這也給予 OSPO 更多與外部單位合作的自由。第二個相近的例子，則是在存在多個產品事業部時，將 OSPO 設在公司層級，並在各事業部設置支援職能。這些支援職能有助於依各事業部的脈絡調整並執行 OSS 策略、政策與流程。第三個例子是虛擬 OSPO，通常會有一位主要負責的 OSS 主管，但沒有完整的專責團隊；而是由不同職能的人員以兼職方式處理相關任務，並由 OSS 主管協調。第四個例子則是沒有正式的 OSPO，而是將相關任務分散給多位人員負責，這是較小型組織適合採用的選項。第五個也是最後一個例子，是將 OSPO 設為技術長辦公室或工程組織的一部分，適合中型組織採用（Haddad，2020）。 ### 2.3. 產業中 OSPO 內部的角色 如同結構與組織位置，OSPO 的人員配置也取決於其目標與目的。Haddad（2020）區分出五種不同角色，但也強調這些角色不一定需要由不同人員分別擔任。相反地，視 OSPO 的結構而定，這些角色可以共享或整併。角色包括： • OSS 主管負責設計與執行 組織的 的動機相當多元，但整體而言，大家越來越承認 OSS 對公部門至關重要，而且從 IT 基礎設施到電子化政府服務，OSS 已經被用在各種場景中。Herpig（2023）特別強調資安的重要性，以及建立資安 OSPO 的必要；美國網路安全暨基礎設施安全局（CISA）的《開放原始碼軟體安全路線圖》（CISA, 2023）也提出同樣建議。主要任務包括監測國家層級的 OSS 供應鏈、推廣 OSS 安全實務、為政策制定者提供建議、支持 OSS 基礎設施發展，以及與更廣泛的 OSS 生態系互動。這些建議也符合 OSS 與 OSPO 政治環境的整體變化，也就是越來越重視軟體供應鏈安全，以及能否依據在地需求、價值與法律，做出技術來源選擇與設計決策（OpenForum Europe, 2022a）。從更一般性的角度來看，OpenForum Europe（2022b）與 Linux Foundation（The TODO Group, 2024c）都強調，公部門組織（PSO）之間共享與再利用軟體，是最有可能帶來效益的方向。這些效益包括經濟成長（Blind et al., 2021）、競爭力與創業成長提升（Nagle, 2023; Wright et al., 2023），以及長期互通性（European Commission, 2017a）；它們也構成潛在政策介入的目標。因此，若干報告也提出政策建議，包括建立 OSPO，且其關注範圍不只限於資安這個特定議題（Herpig, 2023; CISA, 2023）。Mission Bothorel（Mission Bothorel, 2021）報告曾以法國脈絡提出設置 OSPO 的建議；不久後，這項建議也透過法國跨部會數位局（Direction interministérielle du Numérique - La DINUM）下的自由軟體單位實際落地。 在美國脈絡下，也曾提出類似提案（Nagle, 2022），主張設立一個聯邦政府的開源計畫辦公室（OSPO），目標是協調開放原始碼軟體（OSS）政策與其他公部門 OSPO，同時監督並提供 OSS 政策介入措施的一般實施建議，並在國際層級上作為整體 OSS 生態系與其他 OSPO 的對接窗口。 ### 2.6. OSPO 之外的政策實施與支持倡議 若跳脫 OSPO 這個架構來看，已有多次報告指出各種需求與倡議之間的重疊與對齊。以下我們回顧常見挑戰，以及被強調為可用來因應這些挑戰的組織做法。 #### 2.6.1. OSS 採用的挑戰與障礙 數位政府研究讓人注意到，政府與公部門組織（PSOs）在 OSS 與開放協作方面，既有相關機會（Mergel, 2015, 2016），也有相關挑戰（Shaikh, 2016；Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015）。需要關注的挑戰可概括為 The Journal of Systems & Software 241 (2026) 112998 4 **圖 1。根據相關研究建立的概念架構概覽（Haddad, 2020）。與結構相關的類別於第 2.2 節說明，且** 第 2.4 節中的責任相關類別，橫跨多個面向。文化是高度被引用的因素，其特徵是風險趨避且保守的採購實務（Persson and Linåker, 2024），偏好維持現狀（Rossi et al., 2006）與既有解決方案（Deller and Guilloux, 2008; Silic and Back, 2017）。內部溝通與組織層級，也可能導致公共部門組織（PSO）內部採用速度緩慢，甚至完全沒有採用（Cassell, 2008）。在取得與採購過程中，考量開源軟體（OSS）所需的知識與能力不足，也一再被指出（Cassell, 2008; Deller and Guilloux, 2008）。這延續了公共部門長期依賴外包來維持並擴展技術能力、以滿足當前需求的歷史趨勢（Marco-Simó and Pastor-Collado, 2020; Cinar et al., 2019）；這個趨勢在地方政府中特別明顯（Persson and Linåker, 2024）。這導致整個公共部門普遍缺乏技術與軟體工程專業，不只是 OSS 領域如此（Borg et al., 2018）。為了填補這項空缺，供應商與服務提供者至關重要；但其可取得性各有差異（Deller and Guilloux, 2008），也常被視為 OSS 採用的障礙（Cassell, 2008; Koloniaris et al., 2018）。PSO 被描述為對 OSS 社群能提供的支援抱持懷疑（Deller and Guilloux, 2008; Koloniaris et al., 2018），因此專業支援對於整體推動 OSS 採用至關重要（Lungo and Kaasbøl, 2007）。 #### 2.6.2. 類 OSPO 的挑戰與障礙因應方式 無論在中央（Oram, 2011）或地方政府層級（Shaikh, 2016），都需要培養內部技術專業與能力。文獻也明確指出，需要內部的推動者與倡議者，也就是所謂的邊界跨越者（boundary spanners）（Van Loon and Toshkov, 2015）；他們可以提升組織對開源軟體（OSS）相關機會與風險的認識，並作為通往更廣泛 OSS 生態系與相關利害關係人的橋梁，促進信任與知識轉移。這些推動者可以擔任內部顧問，在整個公部門組織（PSO）內提供支持，也能協助那些已有積極協作與夥伴關係的單位（Shaikh, 2016）。這些專家與支援功能，與開源計畫辦公室（OSPO）的概念高度契合（Ruff, 2022），也呼應產業界所表達的需求：組織需要培養能力，以支援符合業務目標的 OSS 營運。對資源有限的地方政府與 PSO 而言，建立專責 OSPO 的意願與預算未必會是優先事項。在這些情況下，共享資源並建立協作架構，在經濟上是合理的（Marco-Simó and Pastor-Collado, 2020），也屬於一般 OSS 協作中的標準做法（O’Mahony, 2005）。例如，丹麥、瑞典與瓦隆等脈絡中已有相關案例報告，顯示地方政府如何透過會員驅動的正式（Frey, 2023）與非正式（Persson and Linåker, 2024）協會、共同擁有的公共服務提供者（Viseur and Jullien, 2023），或由資源較充足的 PSO 擔任 OSS 專案主要贊助者與促成者（Linåker et al., 2025）來進行協作。文獻強調專業支持的必要性，因為地方政府即使已經組織起來，仍特別缺乏技術能力。相關案例（例如 Frey, 2023）強調，必須促成「由中小企業構成的健康生態系，為公部門開源產品提供服務」，以確保能取得「詳細文件、品質保證、認證機制、訓練與支援服務」（Shaikh, 2016）。這些協會以及 OSPO，可以作為相關 PSO 與供應商之間對話與關係的介面與促成者，用來監督並支持「開源做法，使原始碼能在政府內部重複使用」，並確保開發遵循開放且敏捷的實務（Mergel, 2016）。 例子顯示，軟性的供應商鎖定很容易成為現實（Persson and Linåker, 2024）。 ### 2.7. 概念架構 以下提出本文的概念架構（見圖 1），用以刻畫公共部門組織（PSO）內的開源專案辦公室（OSPO），並捕捉其各種實務做法與挑戰；同時也為公共部門組織提供建議，說明它們可如何考慮設立自己的 OSPO。具體而言，預期會有一組與 Haddad（2020）研究類似的原型與責任分工，但其特徵會不同於產業脈絡。 ## 3. 研究設計 本研究提出一項探索性的質性調查（Melegati et al., 2024），探討如何透過組織支持功能或專業能力中心，並以 OSPO 這一建制為核心，明確促成開源軟體（OSS）的採用、開發與協作。更具體地說，本研究將 OSPO 視為一種制度化的組織建制，用以支持並加速 ...
